# Searching by file type in ripgrep

When you run ripgrep across a big folder, you often only care about a few kinds
of file. If you are hunting for a phrase in the HTML pages and want to ignore
everything else, ripgrep can do that for you without you having to name each
file. It knows about more than 200 kinds of file out of the box, and it lets you
teach it new ones. This guide covers the four flags that make it work: `--type`,
`--type-not`, `--type-add` and `--type-list`.

## Search only one kind of file: `--type`

A *type* is just a name ripgrep gives to a set of files. `rust` means Rust
files, `html` means HTML files, and so on. To search only files of one type, add
`--type` followed by the name:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

There is a shorthand, `-t`, and you can pack the name right onto it:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The value of a type is that one name can stand for several file extensions at
once. C files, for example, come in both source (`.c`) and header (`.h`)
flavours. Instead of spelling both out, you search the `c` type:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

You can pass `--type` more than once to search several types together.

There is one special name, `all`. `--type all` searches every file ripgrep
recognises as belonging to *some* type, and nothing else. This is a useful way
to say "search all the real source and document files here, but skip anything
unfamiliar".

## Skip a kind of file: `--type-not`

The opposite flag is `--type-not`, shortened to `-T`. It excludes a type instead
of including it. So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means
"exclude files of this type":

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

Like `--type`, you can repeat `--type-not`, and you can mix the two in one
command to include some types while excluding others.

`--type-not all` is the mirror image of `--type all`: it searches only files
ripgrep does *not* recognise. If you have a folder full of known formats plus a
few odd, extensionless files, `--type-not all` finds the odd ones.

A small but useful detail: types are matched by file-name patterns, so a shell
script named `my-shell-script` with no `.sh` on the end is not counted as the
`sh` type. Both `--type sh` and `--type all` would skip it, while `--type-not
all` would search it.

## See what ripgrep knows: `--type-list`

To find out which types exist and which files each one covers, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line: the name, a colon, then the comma-separated
patterns it matches. You can pipe that through ripgrep itself to find one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

This is the list to check whenever you are unsure of a type's name or want to
know exactly what it includes. It also reflects any types you have added or
changed on the same command line, so it is a good way to confirm a custom type
before you rely on it.

## Make your own type: `--type-add`

If you regularly search a group of files that ripgrep has no name for, define
your own type with `--type-add`. You give it a name, a colon, and a pattern.
Say you often search "web" files, meaning HTML, CSS and JavaScript:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That command invents a type called `web`, then immediately uses it with `-tweb`
to search for `title`. You can add one pattern per `--type-add`, and repeat the
flag to build up a type from several patterns. Type names may use only letters
and numbers.

You can also build a type out of existing ones with `include`. To make a `src`
type covering C++, Python and Markdown:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc TODO
```

One thing to keep in mind: a type you add this way lasts only for that single
command. ripgrep does not remember it. If you want a type available every time,
put the `--type-add` in a shell alias or in your ripgrep configuration file:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

## A note on which filter wins

Type filters are gentle. If you also use an explicit `--glob` pattern, or a file
is excluded by an ignore file, those take priority over your `--type` choice. In
day-to-day searching this rarely surprises you, but it is worth knowing when a
type search returns fewer files than you expected.
